scenes.title: Sessionization
scenes.narration: Sessionization groups a stream of user events into distinct sessions, splitting them wherever a period of inactivity crosses a chosen timeout.

scenes.title: What a session is
bullets: A session is a burst of activity from one user with no long pauses
A common rule: start a new session after 30 minutes of inactivity
Events are per-user, ordered by timestamp
The goal is to assign a session id to every event
scenes.narration: A session is a contiguous burst of activity from a single user with no long gaps in between. A very common rule is that thirty minutes of inactivity ends the current session and any later event begins a new one. We process events per user, ordered by their timestamp, and our goal is to tag every event with a session identifier so we can later count and analyze sessions.

scenes.title: The LAG plus cumulative-sum pattern
steps: Use LAG to fetch each event's previous timestamp for the same user
Compute the gap between the current and previous event
Flag a new session with 1 when the gap exceeds the timeout, else 0
Take a cumulative SUM of those flags to build the session id
scenes.narration: The standard pattern combines LAG with a cumulative sum. First, LAG retrieves the timestamp of each user's previous event so we can measure the gap since it. When that gap exceeds our timeout, we emit a flag of one, marking the first event of a new session, otherwise zero. Finally, a running cumulative sum of those flags produces a session number that increments each time a new session begins.

scenes.title: Flagging new sessions
scenes.code:
SELECT
    user_id,
    event_time,
    CASE
        WHEN event_time - LAG(event_time) OVER (
                 PARTITION BY user_id
                 ORDER BY event_time
             ) > INTERVAL '30 minutes'
          OR LAG(event_time) OVER (
                 PARTITION BY user_id
                 ORDER BY event_time
             ) IS NULL
        THEN 1 ELSE 0
    END AS is_new_session
FROM events;
scenes.narration: This first step flags where sessions begin. For each event, LAG partitioned by user and ordered by time gives the previous event's timestamp. If the difference exceeds thirty minutes, we output a one to mark a new session. We also emit a one when the previous timestamp is null, since a user's very first event always starts a session. Every other event gets a zero.

scenes.title: Building the session id
scenes.code:
WITH flagged AS (
    SELECT
        user_id,
        event_time,
        CASE
            WHEN event_time - LAG(event_time) OVER w
                 > INTERVAL '30 minutes'
              OR LAG(event_time) OVER w IS NULL
            THEN 1 ELSE 0
        END AS is_new_session
    FROM events
    WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time)
)
SELECT
    user_id,
    event_time,
    SUM(is_new_session) OVER (
        PARTITION BY user_id
        ORDER BY event_time
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING
                 AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS session_id
FROM flagged
ORDER BY user_id, event_time;
scenes.narration: Now we turn the flags into session ids. The CTE reuses the flagging logic, tidied with a named WINDOW clause so we do not repeat the partition and order. In the outer query, a cumulative SUM of the flags per user assigns each event a session id: it stays the same within a session and increments by one every time a new-session flag appears. The result is a clean per-user session number attached to every event.

scenes.text: LAG measures the gap, a CASE flags session starts, and a cumulative SUM of those flags numbers the sessions. This three-step recipe sessionizes any event stream.
scenes.narration: Remember the three-step recipe: LAG measures the gap between events, a CASE flags the session starts, and a cumulative sum of those flags numbers the sessions for any event stream.
